newsitem.title: CANADA: EMU delay, forex volatility scorned at ACI confab.
newsitem.headline: EMU delay, forex volatility scorned at ACI confab.

text.p: Central bankers warned against a delay in Europe's planned single currency and pleaded for foreign exchange market stability on Friday as the 39th congress of the Association Cambiste Internationale got into full swing.

"I personally think that postponement is not a good idea," said Bundesbank council member Wendelin Hartmann, speaking to currency dealers at the annual foreign exchange market trade association gathering.

His remarks came against a backdrop of rising EMU jitters across the Atlantic, where a row between the German government and its central bank over Bonn's plan to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves reached a fever pitch.
Hartmann said on Friday that the plan to revalue the central bank's assets could undermine the credibility of Europe's planned currency union.
But the remarks offered currency traders, wandering through the conference hall and sampling the latest in foreign exchange-related technology from exhibitors, little to cheer about.
The industry is struggling in the face of declining volatility in major currencies, industry consolidation and the worrisome implications of a single European currency.

A poll of delegates to the conference revealed that 13 of 15 dealers saw the German debate having little impact on the start date to monetary union, with some predicting an easier path toward monetary union and others a more inclusive group of founding members as a result of the gold plan.
"If Germany goes ahead with the revaluation it can hardly turn round to others and tell them they can't do similar things," said one trader at a U.S. bank.

Traders also found little solace in the remarks of William McDonough, President of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, who addressed industry concerns about the long-term trend toward declining volatility in the currency markets.
"Foreign exchange rates are fundamentally determined by market forces and should be free to fluctuate as a vital adjustment mechanism for the global economy," McDonough noted.
"However, excessive volatility, like price instability, can diminish resources otherwise available for productive growth."

Though large foreign exchange rate fluctuations have been a boon to volatility-starved dealers in recent months, the trend over the past several years has been one of greater stability -- leading to declining profits for currency desks.
"Volatility is the bread and butter for traders and banks themselves," Theo van Koningsveld, a senior vice president at Rabobank International who attended McDonough's speech said.
"In reality traders are eager for any volatility in any currency they can find."
Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen, the first speaker of the day, gave those traders who were not attending the conference a reason to buy Canadian dollars on Friday.

Thiessen said prospects were good for the Canadian dollar to strengthen over time for cyclical and fundamental reasons. Given past monetary easing, he noted that prospects were good for continued robust expansion in the Canadian economy through 1997 and into 1998.
His remarks pushed the Canadian dollar to a higher close ahead of a general election scheduled for Monday.

The conference wraps up on Saturday, when former Japanese Ministry of Finance official Toyoo Gyohten and Chilean Finance Minister Eduardo Amimat are scheduled to speak about the outlooks for Asia and Latin America, respectively.
